In November 2025 it acquired Ocean Fish Group, a fishing and processing business in Cornwall, England, having bought tug operator Holyhead Towing in Anglesey, Wales, the previous year.

World.title: An Argentine consultant who advised Milei's campaign detained in Bolivia after a shooting
World.content:
An Argentine consultant who advised Milei's campaign detained in Bolivia after a shooting

19th Wednesday, August 2026 - 09:52 UTC Full article

The 33-year-old lawyer underwent surgery and survived; none of the rounds struck vital organs. The case is being investigated as attempted femicide

Bolivian police detained Argentine political consultant Fernando Cerimedo in the early hours of Tuesday at Viru Viru international airport in Santa Cruz de la Sierra, hours after his former partner, Bolivian lawyer Nadia Beller, was shot three times outside a hotel in the city. Cerimedo has not been formally charged and his involvement in the attack, which remains under investigation, has not been established.

The departmental police commander for Santa Cruz, David Gómez, said investigators had information about the consultant's movements and deployed officers at the airport. He said a prior falling-out between the two was among the lines of inquiry. “Days ago Ms Beller and Mr Cerimedo are said to have had a relationship problem,” he said. The detainee was handed over to the Special Anti-Crime Force.

Security cameras recorded the attack, which took place on Monday night in the city's business district. Two men dressed as food delivery riders got off a motorcycle, shot Beller at the hotel entrance and took her bag and phone before fleeing. The 33-year-old lawyer underwent surgery and survived; none of the rounds struck vital organs. The case is being investigated as attempted femicide.

From hospital, Beller said she had been summoned to the location on a pretext linked to a legal case and that she feigned death to avoid being finished off. She accused Cerimedo of having tried to strangle her on two occasions since their relationship began in late 2025, said she is four weeks pregnant and requested protection. She also said she has knowledge of alleged corruption within President Rodrigo Paz's circle. No charges have been brought over any of these allegations and the government has not responded to them.

Government Minister Marco Antonio Oviedo called for “a serious and thorough investigation” and said that in Bolivia “nobody is above the law.” Vice-President Edman Lara described the episode as an attack “against life, democracy and freedom of expression.”

Cerimedo co-founded the digital outlet La Derecha Diario and took part in the social media strategy behind Javier Milei's 2023 presidential campaign. He also worked for Jair Bolsonaro and was investigated by Brazilian courts over the dissemination of claims of fraud in the 2022 elections, a case from which he was cleared. He advised Paz's campaign and retains a link to his government, although the Bolivian executive maintains he is not part of the state structure. In July, the then minister of the presidency, José Luis Lupo, said his consultancy is funded with external resources.

Beller stood as a candidate for the Movement Towards Socialism in 2019 and in recent years has worked as a political analyst critical of that party.

World.title: Australia launches program to vaccinate colonies of little penguins against avian influenza
World.content:
Australia launches program to vaccinate colonies of little penguins against avian influenza

19th Wednesday, August 2026 - 08:45 UTC Full article

Operations will be conducted at night when the penguins return from the sea and are directed to a special area where they will receive the first dose

According to ABC News Australia wildlife conservation agencies in the state of Victoria have launched a program to vaccinate little penguins against the H5 strain of avian influenza. Over the next few weeks, experts plan to capture and vaccinate more than 5,000 birds in colonies on Philip Island and St. Kilda.

The virus, first detected in southwestern Victoria about two and a half weeks ago, has spread to Philip Island. On the eve of the vaccination campaign, the death of a little penguin from the virus was confirmed. The bird was found in a different part of the island, away from the site of the nightly tourist penguin watch.

The colony on Phillip Island numbers up to 40,000 birds and is one of the largest in the world. A state government study released in May 2025 modeled the risks of H5N1 to this population and predicted that, in a worst-case scenario, between 8,000 and 16,000 penguins could die. Little penguins are vulnerable to the spread of infection because they nest and gather in large groups.

Victoria’s Chief Biodiversity Officer, James Todd, stated that operations will be conducted at night. When the penguins return from the sea, they will be directed to a special area where they will receive their first dose of the vaccine and be microchipped, after which the birds will be able to return to their burrows. The number of staff will be limited to reduce biosafety risks to both people and animals.

According to Todd, vaccinating wild animals is complicated by the need for two doses of the vaccine, which is usually impractical or impossible. Priority will be given to penguins participating in the tourist “penguin parade”: they are accustomed to people and have predictable movement patterns. The nightly shows for visitors will continue for now.

Jack Gough, a representative of the Invasive Species Council, called Philip Island likely the best-prepared location in Australia, but noted that vaccination should have begun earlier. Todd emphasized that the detection of the virus in the little penguin is cause for concern, but experts advise continuing the vaccination program as quickly and safely as possible. Officials are also considering expanding the program to include vulnerable animal species in captivity.

World.title: Is Mexico really dangerous? Why travel advisories don’t tell the whole story
World.content:
If you’ve ever mentioned an upcoming trip to a friend or family member, chances are someone’s told you to “check the travel advisory.”

And they’re not wrong.

Travel advisories exist for a reason. They can provide genuinely important information about crime, political unrest, natural disasters, health concerns and other risks that could affect your trip.

But there’s a problem with the way we sometimes use them. We treat a travel advisory as though it were a map, but it isn’t. It’s more of a compass. It can point you toward areas where you need to pay attention, but it can’t tell you what life looks like on every street, in every city or for every traveler.

A vast country of distinct realities

Mexico is a perfect example of why context matters.

Mexico is enormous. It’s a country full of numerous different realities. It stretches from the Pacific to the Caribbean, from deserts in the north to tropics in the south, with sprawling cities, tiny mountain villages, beach communities, agricultural regions and everything in between.

So, when someone asks me, “But isn’t Mexico dangerous?” my first question is usually, “Where in Mexico?” Because that’s a very different question.

I live in Bucerías, just outside of Puerto Vallarta, but I’ve also traveled the country extensively. Places like Guanajuato, Guadalajara, León, Puebla and Mexico City each have their own personalities, challenges and rhythms.

Walking around a busy neighborhood in Mexico City isn’t the same experience as traveling through a remote rural area. The concerns you might have visiting one state may be completely irrelevant in another. Yet when someone sees a headline about crime or a government advisory warning about Mexico, the entire country suddenly becomes one giant red zone in their imagination.

That’s not really how countries work, though.

Imagine issuing a single travel warning for the United States based on what happens in Chicago, New Orleans, Detroit or a particular border region, and then applying that warning equally to someone visiting a small town in Vermont. It wouldn’t make much sense.

The same principle applies to Mexico.

Broad tools rather than local guides

Government advisories are deliberately cautious, and they should be. The U.S., U.K., Canada, Australia and other governments have systems designed to warn their citizens about potential risks abroad. Those warnings can be incredibly useful, particularly when there’s a serious and immediate threat. But they’re broad tools. They aren’t designed to tell you whether the café you’re planning to visit is safe, whether the neighborhood around your hotel feels comfortable or whether a demonstration taking place hundreds of kilometers away is likely to affect your weekend.

That’s where the rest of your research comes in.

A national warning should be the beginning of the conversation, not the end of it.

If an advisory makes you nervous, don’t simply cancel the trip. Dig a little deeper. Look at the specific region you’re visiting. Many governments provide much more detailed information once you get beyond the headline.

Check local news and see what’s actually happening in the city or state you’re planning to visit. Talk to people who live there or have recently traveled there, and check embassy or consulate notices for local developments, demonstrations, weather events or transportation disruptions.

It’s also worth thinking about the kind of traveler you are. Someone traveling alone through a remote region with little Spanish and limited access to transportation has a very different risk profile from someone staying in an established tourist area with reliable transport and plenty of local support.

Neither is necessarily right or wrong. They’re simply different.

Acknowledging risk without assuming danger

Living here has made me much more aware of the difference between acknowledging risk and assuming danger. It’s taught me to look at the whole picture.

Crime exists in Mexico. Of course it does. So do hurricanes, earthquakes, protests, road accidents, medical emergencies and all the other things that can go wrong when you’re traveling anywhere. But those realities don’t automatically define every person’s experience.

I’d never tell anyone to ignore an official warning. Quite the opposite. If multiple governments are warning against travel to a particular region because of serious, ongoing threats, pay attention. If there are reports of targeted attacks, widespread unrest or a major natural disaster, that’s not the moment to decide you’re going to prove everyone wrong. Being adventurous doesn’t require being reckless. But neither does being cautious require being afraid of an entire country.

Why government advice varies

One thing I’ve always found interesting is comparing travel advisories from different countries. They don’t always say exactly the same thing. That’s not necessarily because one is right and another is wrong. Governments have different thresholds, different information and different approaches to risk.

If several governments are highlighting the same specific threat, that’s certainly worth taking seriously. If their advice differs considerably, though, that’s a reason to investigate further.

The goal isn’t to find the advisory that tells you what you want to hear. It’s to understand why the advice differs.

Practical details and insurance fine print

There are also plenty of risks that have nothing to do with crime, so don’t dismiss the practical stuff. What will the weather be like? Are there hurricanes or extreme heat at that time of year? How good is medical care where you’re going? Will you have reliable transportation? Are there areas where cell service is limited? What happens if you get sick or stranded?

And check your travel insurance. That one is particularly important because some policies have exclusions related to government travel warnings. A destination being somewhere you can travel doesn’t necessarily mean your insurance will cover you if you’re traveling against official advice. So read the fine print before you need it.

Informed decisions over absolute fear

There’s no such thing as completely risk-free travel. There isn’t even such a thing as a completely risk-free life. We accept a certain amount of risk every time we get into a car, cross a road, fly somewhere or try something unfamiliar. Travel is about managing that risk intelligently rather than pretending it doesn’t exist.

Places change. Situations change. Advisories change. That’s why context matters.

A destination that appears in a warning today may look very different six months or a year from now. And a country that’s broadly considered safe can still contain places where travelers should exercise considerable caution. The important thing is knowing the difference.

So yes, check the travel advisory. Please do! But then keep reading to better understand the risks that apply to you, rather than simply the risks attached to an entire country.

Travel advisories are there to help us make informed decisions, not to make those decisions for us. Let them point you toward the questions you need to ask, because being a smart traveler isn’t about eliminating every possible risk. It’s about understanding where the risks are, preparing for them and making an informed decision about whether the experience is worth it.

And sometimes, once you’ve looked beyond the headline, you discover something quite wonderful. The place you were warned about isn’t necessarily the place you imagined. It’s a real place, filled with real people, complicated realities, beautiful moments and stories you never would have found on a government website.

Charlotte Smith is a writer and journalist based in Mexico. Her work focuses on travel, politics and community. You can follow along with her travel stories at www.salsaandserendipity.com.

World.title: An infamous Morelos narco ranch will be converted into a school and health center
World.content:
A ranch in central Mexico formerly owned by convicted drug kingpin Edgar Valdez Villarreal — aka “La Barbie” — will be converted into a high school and health complex, Morelos Gov. Margarita González Saravia said Tuesday.

The property, known as El Paraíso, is in Atlacholoaya, roughly a 35-minute drive south of Cuernavaca, the Morelos state capital.

will house three entities: a technological agricultural high school; a center for traditional medicine; and an office of a 2-year-old state agency that promotes and supports Indigenous and Afro-Mexican communities.

The school, known by its Spanish initials CBTA, is intended to address a longstanding demand for secondary education infrastructure in the area. Its curriculum will be tied to traditional medicine and ancestral knowledge held by Morelos’ Indigenous communities.

Construction and renovation work is expected to begin in the coming weeks.

Authorities seized the property after Valdez’s former associate Arturo Beltrán Leyva was killed by Mexican Navy personnel in a 2009 raid of a Cuernavaca apartment complex.

The leader of the Beltrán Leyva organization at the time, Beltrán and his brothers had been senior figures in the Sinaloa Cartel before breaking away.

The ranch was later transferred to Indep, the federal agency that administers and disposes of assets seized by the government.

The National Lottery offered El Paraíso as one of 22 prizes in a 2021 raffle that also included drug lord Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán’s former safe house, homes, land and a luxury box at Estadio Azteca. The money raised was to support federal social programs, such as assistance for Olympic and Paralympic athletes.

More than 773,000 tickets sold nationwide for 250 pesos each (about US $12.60 at that time), and a woman from Jojutla in southern Morelos won the ranch.

However, Nereida Morales declined to take possession, citing the ranch’s deterioration and the maintenance costs. She later agreed to sell the property to the Morelos government for an undisclosed price.

The property was valued at 61.43 million pesos (US $3.1 million) for the lottery drawing.

Valdez, 53, was born in Laredo, Texas, in 1973. Nicknamed “La Barbie” for his blond hair and blue eyes, he was arrested in Mexico in 2010 and extradited to the United States in 2015.

He pleaded guilty to four drug-trafficking counts and one money-laundering count and in 2018 was sentenced to 49 years and one month in federal prison.

Court records later showed that Valdez had provided information to U.S. authorities while he was still a trafficker, including allegations that officials in former President Felipe Calderón’s administration had aided drug cartels.

In 2022, the Bureau of Prisons said Valdez was no longer in its custody but declined to disclose his location. That prompted speculation he was cooperating with U.S. authorities, but officials never confirmed that. A 2025 Justice Department release continued to list his 49-year sentence.

With reports from Animal Político and Diario de Morelos

World.title: What is President Sheinbaum’s view on Mexico becoming a data center hub?
World.content:
As data centers proliferate in Mexico, President Sheinbaum has taken a nuanced stand that recognizes the need for the centers but is skeptical about the country becoming a hub for them.

During her Tuesday morning press conference, Sheinbaum said she believes Mexico needs data centers to develop artificial intelligence (AI) but opposes becoming a “global data center” to meet external demand.

“We do need to have data centers to advance in artificial intelligence, but Mexico does not necessarily have to be the data center for other parts of the world, because it requires high energy and water consumption,” Sheinbaum said.

In Querétaro — which continues to lead AI expansion in Mexico — the debate has intensified precisely due to the potential pressure on strategic resources.

When asked about alleged power outages that had stalled data center investments in Querétaro, Sheinbaum cited reports from the Federal Electricity Commission (CFE) showing such complaints have decreased. She also noted that investment is needed primarily in transmission and distribution, rather than in generation.

New data center facilities continue to arrive in the state, as well as in other parts of the country.

Indeed, according to market research firm Arizton, by January of this year, Mexico hosted some 47 data centers, mainly located in Querétaro, Mexico City and Guanajuato, with 12 more in the pipeline.

Just last week, KIO Data Centers announced it would invest up to US $1.3 billion to develop a new data center in Querétaro with the objective of meeting regional demand for cloud and AI infrastructure.

Although Sheinbaum acknowledged that data centers play an important role in the country’s modernization, their contribution to employment is low and their environmental impact is high.

“[Data centers] do generate economic growth, but with very little job creation and high consumption of natural resources,” Sheinbaum said, adding that her government is also prioritizing other sectors, such as manufacturing, which generate more jobs and place less pressure on natural resources.

Sheinbaum stressed that Mexico should develop the data centers it needs for AI through careful planning that considers the country’s technology needs, electricity infrastructure, natural resource constraints and job creation, rather than be driven by global demand.

With reports from La Jornada and Infobae

World.title: 9 alleged CJNG members arrested in Michoacán security operation
World.content:
Federal security forces on Wednesday arrested nine alleged members of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) in Michoacán. Among those detained was one woman identified as the daughter of a CJNG regional boss and another woman identified as the partner of the same man.

The CJNG responded to the federal operation by blocking highways in Michoacán at more than 20 points, including by setting vehicles on fire, but most, if not all, of the narco-blockades had been cleared by early Wednesday afternoon.

The Ministry of National Defense (Defensa) said in a statement that “nine members of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel” were arrested in Tinaja de Vargas and Colesio, towns in the municipalities of Tanhuato and Ecuandureo, respectively. Those municipalities are located in northwestern Michoacán near the state’s border with Jalisco.

Defensa said that Mexican Army special forces and the National Guard carried out the operation in Michoacán “in coordination with” the federal Security Ministry, the Federal Attorney General’s Office and the Mexican Navy. Military intelligence work facilitated the location of the suspects.

Defensa said that Marisol “N” and Lourdes “N” were among the nine people arrested. The ministry said that the former has been identified as a daughter of Heraclio “N” (Heraclio Guerrero Martínez) while the latter has been identified as his “romantic partner.”

Defensa said that Guerrero, known as “Tío Lako,” is a CJNG “regional boss” in Michoacán and Jalisco. It also said he is “responsible for ordering attacks on National Guard troops” on Feb. 22, 2026, after the arrest of former CJNG leader Rubén “El Mencho” Oseguera Cervantes, who was fatally wounded by military personnel during the operation to capture him.

Wednesday morning’s operation apparently targeted Guerrero, but the alleged cartel boss managed to avoid arrest.

Defensa said that two properties were secured during the operation and authorities seized 64 vehicles, one of which was armored; five machine guns; nine long guns; a handgun; two grenade launcher attachments; ammunition and magazines; drugs; eight improvised explosive devices; seven motorcycles; a drone; and tactical equipment.

The ministry said that the nine detained suspects were flown by a Mexican Air Force helicopter to Mexico City, where they were handed over to the Federal Attorney General’s Office.

Narco-blockades in Michoacán

Defensa noted that there were “various interruptions” to highways in Michoacán after the nine alleged CJNG members were arrested. Civilian and military authorities consequently activated “the Anti-blockade Plan” in order to “guarantee freedom of movement” in the state, the ministry said.

Presumed cartel members set up narco-blockades on highways in various municipalities of Michoacán, including Morelia, Zamora, La Piedad, Chilchota and Ecuandureo. Vehicles, including trucks and buses, were set on fire to create the blockades. Criminal groups in Mexico often create narco-blockades to impede security forces. The setting alight of vehicles is also a show of force for cartels as well as a demonstration of their anger over the arrest of one or more of their members.

⭕️ Al menos 12 bloqueos carreteros con vehículos incendiados fueron reportados en diez municipios de #Michoacán, informaron fuentes policiacas. Los cierres iniciaron alrededor de las 6:00 horas, tras un operativo de fuerzas federales contra un presunto líder del cártel Jalisco… pic.twitter.com/DQMz6bpZB2 — La Jornada (@lajornadaonline) August 19, 2026

Michoacán’s C5 security command center reported on social media that 26 blockades set up in Michoacán on Wednesday morning had been cleared by 12:30 p.m.

Earlier in the day, Michoacán Governor Alfredo Ramírez noted that blockades at nine different locations had been cleared.

“We’re maintaining a permanent presence on the highways to guarantee your safety and to keep traffic moving smoothly,” he wrote on X.

“I ask that you drive carefully, follow the instructions of authorities, and consult only official sources,” Ramírez said.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: García Harfuch earns DEA administrator’s praise at anti-drug trafficking conference
World.content:
Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) Administrator Terrance “Terry” Cole publicly praised Security Minister Omar García Harfuch during this week’s 40th International Drug Enforcement Conference (IDEC) in Buenos Aires, Argentina, describing him as a “trusted partner” and a “good friend of the United States.”

Addressing representatives from more than 100 countries, Cole gave an overview of García Harfuch’s career with the Federal Police, Mexico’s Criminal Investigation Agency (AIC) and the Mexico City Security Ministry, prior to leading the Security and Citizen Protection Ministry. “Secretary Harfuch has devoted nearly two decades to public service to protect people in Mexico,” he said.

🤝🇲🇽🇺🇸 “García Harfuch es socio de confianza y buen amigo de Estados Unidos”. – Terry Cole / Administrador de la DEA #SegurosJuntos 🛡️🤝 pic.twitter.com/gYr6hupAfd — Embajada de EE.UU. en México (@USEmbassyMEX) August 19, 2026

Cole highlighted that the Mexican official is personally familiar with the risks of combating transnational criminal organizations, recalling the attack by the CJNG that he survived in June 2020.

He also noted that García Harfuch understands the importance of sharing intelligence, targeting criminal leaders, disrupting supply chains and dismantling networks from the top down.

In a separate speech, García Harfuch addressed the collaboration between the two countries, under which U.S. agencies are processing 155 arrest warrants for extradition purposes related to investigations by agencies in the neighboring country.

He said that 14 individuals — either wanted or considered priority targets by the FBI — have been arrested in connection with investigations into drug trafficking, homicide, money laundering, human trafficking and other activities of transnational criminal organizations.

Regarding financial matters, García Harfuch stated that Mexico’s Financial Intelligence Unit has added more than 2,300 subjects to its List of Blocked Persons, frozen over 8.6 billion pesos in assets (US $507 million) and blocked more than 24,600 accounts.

He also seized the international opportunity to share the numbers resulting from his ministry’s push to reduce violent crime over the past two years: 63,500 people arrested for high-impact crimes, more than 32,800 firearms seized and 518 metric tonnes of drugs confiscated. The number of daily homicides has dropped from 86 to 42, a more than 50% reduction.

En Buenos Aires, Argentina, me encuentro participando en la Conferencia Internacional para el Control de Drogas, donde compartimos los resultados de la Estrategia Nacional de Seguridad que encabeza la Presidenta @Claudiashein y que ha fortalecido las capacidades de inteligencia,… pic.twitter.com/kqGn1H6gpX — Omar H Garcia Harfuch (@OHarfuch) August 18, 2026

From his official X account, García Harfuch posted images of his participation in the Buenos Aires conference and reiterated Mexico’s commitment against international crime.

“Mexico will continue to cooperate with its international partners based on clear principles: shared responsibility, reciprocity, mutual trust and full respect for our sovereignty,” he said.

With reports from Imagen and Proceso

World.title: Mexico is fighting a US antidumping tariff on strawberries
World.content:
Mexico has condemned the U.S. Commerce Department for calling for an antidumping tariff on Mexican strawberries, a move Mexico says would violate international standards and threaten to end decades of largely duty-free strawberry trade between the two countries.

Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard voiced a “grave concern” over a preliminary determination by the U.S. that Mexican strawberry exports were being dumped during the winter season, which, if true, would constitute an unfair trade practice that consists of exporting goods at prices below their production cost or lower than the sales price in the domestic market.

Mexico’s Economy Ministry (SE) issued a statement Tuesday night informing the public that the U.S. accused Mexico of selling strawberries at prices between 3.37% and 5.28% below the normal product value.

To win the case, the U.S. must prove that Mexican strawberry sales are being made below fair value and the International Trade Commission (ITC), an independent quasi-judicial U.S. entity, must agree that the imports could cause material injury to the U.S. industry.

However, Mexico’s SE says that the “arbitrarily applied” U.S. criteria are inconsistent with the ITC Antidumping Agreement and with provisions in the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA).

The case originated on Dec. 31, 2025, when Florida producers requested that the Commerce Department and the ITC impose antidumping duties, based on a differentiation between “strawberries” and “winter strawberries” harvested between Nov. 1 and March 31 and on the existence of a regional market limited to the eastern U.S. states.

The ITC concluded in March that there was no basis for considering winter strawberries as a distinct product from strawberries in general, nor for recognizing a regional market separate from the U.S. national market, according to Mexico’s Economy Ministry. But that conclusion was preliminary and did not halt the proceedings. The final ruling by the ITC is expected in early 2027, either allowing the U.S. to impose antidumping tariffs on Mexico or dismissing the case.

The imposition of tariffs would affect almost 5,000 Mexican strawberry producers — 97% of whom are small or medium-sized, with no more than 10 hectares — and around 151,000 jobs. In 2025, Mexico exported 263,000 metric tons of strawberries to the United States, valued at $1 billion.

On the other hand, from a U.S. industry perspective, Mexican producers are selling winter-harvested strawberries in the United States at prices U.S. producers cannot compete with.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has warned that the U.S. Commerce Department’s determination could set a precedent for other U.S. producers to challenge other Mexican fruit and vegetable exports by dividing products into seasons or delimiting regional markets.

According to the U.S. Department of Agriculture, 98% of U.S. strawberry imports came from Mexico last year. Mexico accounts for 5.9% of global strawberry production, making it the world’s fifth-largest producer.

With reports from El Economista, Expansión, Infobae, CNN and Hortidaily

World.title: Why don’t more foreign tourists come to Central Mexico? MND’s journalism intern explains
World.content:
Nine weeks ago I set out on a mission. I had just arrived in Mexico for a journalism internship in San Miguel de Allende, and was trying to figure out why more foreigners — especially Americans — don’t travel to Central Mexico, and if they should.

Americans make up the majority of international arrivals into Mexico, but most head for the pristine coastline in Cancún, Cabo and Puerto Vallarta. Very few head to the country’s high-elevation center, and even fewer head to places outside of Mexico City.

But they are undoubtedly missing out. Americans tend to make long-haul trips to Europe to eat unique food, explore cobblestone streets and take in thousands of years of history. They can get the same experience with their southern neighbor, so why don’t they come?

Here are some of the reasons I found after living in Mexico for two months.

1. Public perceptions towards Mexico

The most obvious reason is the media perception of Mexico in the United States. Mexico is routinely painted as a hot, dangerous and drug-filled desert that sends millions of illegal immigrants through the northern border.

On Aug. 4, influencer César Gastélum was shot and killed on a live stream in Sinaloa amid ongoing cartel turf wars. The clip spread rapidly on social media, with the most-liked comments all calling Mexico unsafe and warning people to stay away.

Even before I started my internship, I had to go through weeks of safety training. I had friends tell me that they were scared for me and almost everyone questioned if it would be safe. That is the perception of Mexico that many Americans have.

Thirteen of Mexico’s 32 states have a level 3 or 4 advisory by the U.S. State Department, with only two — Campeche and Yucatán — holding a level 1 warning. These warnings and constant headlines of violence in Mexico keep the country off countless American bucket lists.

Mexico has problems, of course. Mexico’s homicide rate is 3-5 times higher than that of the U.S. and organized crime has plagued many states and areas around the country. But Mexico is a giant nation. There are parts I will never set foot in out of fear and parts I already want to go back to.

I grew up in the north suburbs of Chicago. Up there it is perfectly safe. Other parts of the city are not. There are areas of Chicago that I have never been to in my life, and that I never plan to go to. It is the same in Mexico but on a national scale. I will avoid Sinaloa and Ecatepec, but go to Mexico City and Oaxaca. Chicago and Mexico are both victims of clickbait headlines about widespread violence. Don’t believe them. I felt safer in Mexico than near my university in Seattle.

Wherever I went, I saw families playing outside and parties in town squares. The people seemed happy and secure. I do not get that same feeling in many parts of the United States.

2. Less familiarity

When most Americans think of an international vacation, they think of Rome, London, Madrid or Athens. Guanajuato, Querétaro, San Miguel de Allende or Oaxaca usually never cross their minds. There is a long history of Americans crossing the Atlantic for their big vacation, but that does not happen in Central Mexico.

While I met plenty of people who had been to San Miguel before I left, most had never even heard of it, let alone Guanajuato or Querétaro, which get far fewer American visitors.

Americans tend to like to enjoy places where they can be more comfortable, which usually means they flock to where Americans already are. Massive European hubs that have been recommended by countless American tourists to their friends and family will rake in visitors, while Central Mexican destinations — for better or worse — go unnoticed.

Central Mexico will never appear in as many movies (in a positive way, at least) as France or England. It will never be considered as romantic as Italy. So Americans will keep going to Europe.

I’ve been to Europe several times and now I’ve been to Mexico for nine weeks. The lack of familiarity, which is both real and exaggerated, is what made traveling in Mexico so great. I was never craving uniquely American experiences in Mexico. Why would I come to Mexico if I wanted everything to be like the United States?

So yes, there is sometimes a lack of familiarity. I noticed people wearing different clothes and eating different foods. They had different phrases that sometimes made me uncomfortable and they had different customs. But now I understand them and can go back to the U.S. having learned new things. I would not have gotten that if I just went to a place where every person I saw was a tourist.

3. Logistical and language issues

Americans like to speak English. In Central Mexico it’s far more common for people to lead with Spanish, unlike in Cabo or Cancún. For many American travelers, that’s enough to dissuade a visit.

Airport announcements are exclusively in Spanish, as well as signs at bus terminals. Sometimes asking for directions or ordering at a restaurant can be difficult. It can be hard to make conversation or meet acquaintances.

That’s part of the reason why San Miguel gets so many American tourists. You can easily get around with English and the town is relatively well-integrated to Americans. It may sometimes make for a less authentic trip, but one that is much easier to navigate and is more familiar while still having all the charm that Central Mexico provides.

As someone who speaks very limited Spanish, I was worried about the language barrier. Staying in San Miguel made it more seamless, but it was harder to get by when I traveled to Querétaro or Oaxaca. But that discomfort is part of traveling and part of becoming integrated in the culture. I had translation apps on my phone and tried to make an effort to speak in Spanish when I could. That was more than enough to get by.

It often was not easy but it was never that hard. If Spanish is stopping you from taking a trip to Mexico, I’m here to tell you that it shouldn’t. I struggled at times, but without trying to speak Spanish, I would not have been able to experience some of the rewarding experiences that I had.

What you’re missing out on

Colorful cities. Colonial streets. Winding mountain passes and waterfalls. Ancient ruins and cactus gardens. Tacos, tlayudas and empanadas.

Central Mexico truly has it all. I have been grateful to discover it during my nine-week internship. There were many times that I was grateful for streets that felt devoid of Americans, and there were times I was wishing for more familiarity. But that is the beauty of studying abroad.

Americans are missing out on many of the same experiences they can get in Europe. In Mexico, they can travel on a shorter flight and at lower prices. It also comes with learning what the real Mexico is like, which is ever-important as the two countries have been increasingly linked for decades. Over 38 million people of Mexican origin live in the U.S., and nearly two million Americans live in Mexico.

As these two countries seemingly grow apart over political tensions, meeting Mexicans in person and seeing how they truly live their lives has never been so fulfilling. It has also never been so maddening as they continue to be vilified in the United States. I can confidently say that coming to Mexico will be one of the greatest experiences of my college years and one that I will never forget.

Jared Tucker is a summer intern at Mexico News Daily in San Miguel de Allende and a rising senior at the University of Washington in Seattle, where he is the sports editor for The Daily UW. He was previously a fellow at TheFulcrum.us, where he covered public participation in American democracy.

World.title: Mexico and My Money: What you told us about your personal finance habits and hang-ups
World.content:
Thank you to everyone who completed the Mexico News Daily “Mexico and My Money” survey, which sought to gather information about the financial practices and experiences of foreigners living in Mexico.

Almost 700 of you responded to the survey and we have now analyzed the results, which are presented in this article.

Before we get to them, let us remind you that we conducted this survey to help guide and define the topics of a new MND series called “Mexico and My Money.”

The first article in the series, which was introduced by MND CEO Travis Bembenek earlier this month, will be published next week.

The MND ‘Mexico and My Money’ survey results

Who responded?

By our cutoff time, 680 people living in 25 of Mexico’s 32 states had responded to the survey.

The top 10 states where respondents live are Jalisco, Guanajuato, Nayarit, Quintana Roo, Baja California Sur, Mexico City, Yucatán, Oaxaca, Baja California and Sinaloa.

Around 44% of respondents have lived in Mexico for 11 years or longer, while the remaining 56% have lived here for 10 years or less.

The respondents are both full-time (70%) and part-time (30%) residents of Mexico.

Almost eight in ten respondents (79%) are retired, while the remainder work either part-time (11%) or full-time (10%).

More than seven in 10 respondents (73%) own their primary home, while the remainder rent.

10 Key Takeaways

7 in 10 respondents think their money is safe or very safe in banks in Mexico

More than four in 10 respondents (44%) think their money is “safe” in a bank in Mexico while an additional 28% believe their money is “very safe” in a bank in Mexico.

Almost one-quarter of respondents (23.5%) chose the “neutral” option in response to the question about the safety of their deposits in banks in Mexico.

Only 5% of respondents think their money is “unsafe” (4.5%) or “very unsafe” (less than 0.5%) in a bank in Mexico.

One factor that may have influenced people’s perceptions about the safety of their money in banks in Mexico is that federal Finance Minister Édgar Amador Zamora promptly reassured CIBanco and Intercam account holders that their money was “absolutely” safe after the U.S. Department of the Treasury last year accused the banks of laundering millions of dollars for drug cartels, prompting the government to take control of them. For the vast majority of CIBanco and Intercam customers that proved to be the case, although account holders who responded to a previous Mexico News Daily survey did face a range of inconveniences linked to the U.S. accusations.

8 in 10 respondents don’t have a Mexican credit card

Almost 37% of respondents don’t have a checking account based in Mexico, 58% don’t have a savings account with a bank in Mexico and a striking 79% don’t have a credit card issued by a Mexico-based bank.

A strong majority of respondents (72%) do, however, have a debit card issued by a Mexico-based bank.

The results suggest that many foreigners in Mexico use credit cards issued by banks in their countries of origin.

One possible reason why many foreigners opt not to get a credit card from a bank in Mexico is that credit card interest rates are typically very high.

8 of 10 respondents have made some kind of investment in Mexico

Only 21% of respondents have not invested in at least one of real estate, stocks, bonds or a business in Mexico. The remaining 79% of surveyed foreigners have invested in at least one of those assets.

The purchase of a home in Mexico was easily the most popular investment. Seven in 10 respondents (71%) own a home in Mexico, while 14% have a property in which they don’t currently live. Just over 12% of respondents receive rental income from a property they own in Mexico.

One in 10 respondents (10%) has invested in a business in Mexico, while 8% of surveyed foreigners have bought stocks and 9% have purchased bonds.

A strong majority of respondents have not had ‘money issues’ with contractors or other service providers in Mexico

Over eight in ten respondents (83%) of respondents have not had “money issues” with contractors in Mexico.

Almost nine in 10 surveyed foreigners (87%) have not had “money issues” with people who provide regular services to them in Mexico, such as landlords, cleaners or gardeners.

* Read about some of the money issues respondents have experienced with contractors and other service providers in the final section of this article.

Most respondents have not been a victim of a financial crime in Mexico

Over eight in ten respondents (82%) have not been a victim of a financial crime in Mexico, whereas 18% of survey respondents have been a victim of such an offense.

* Read about some of the financial crimes respondents have suffered in the final section of this article.

The vast majority of respondents have not borrowed money from a financial institution in Mexico

Almost 97% of respondents have not borrowed money from a financial institution in Mexico. Just over 3% of surveyed foreigners have borrowed money in Mexico.

This result suggests that the vast majority of respondents purchased real estate, vehicles and other assets in Mexico with their own funds or took out loans abroad.

As is the case with credit cards, the high cost of credit in Mexico is a deterrent to taking out loans in Mexico for many foreigners.

Rising prices in Mexico have negatively affected the lifestyles of 4 in 10 respondents

The increase in prices in Mexico in recent years has negatively affected the lifestyles of around four in ten (38%) respondents.

The lifestyles of the remaining 62% of surveyed foreigners have not been adversely affected by rising prices.

Mexico’s annual headline inflation rate fell to 3.12% in July, the lowest level in more than six years. However, inflation in Mexico was much higher in earlier years of this decade, peaking at an annual headline rate of 8.7% August and September of 2022.

Inflation, combined with other factors such as the strength of the peso, has made life in Mexico considerably more expensive in recent years.

Respondents are, on average, ‘somewhat concerned’ about fluctuations in the USD:MXN exchange rate

MND asked survey respondents to rate their concern over fluctuations in the value of the Mexican peso or the US dollar on a scale of 0 to 100.

On the scale, 0 meant “unconcerned”; 50 signified “somewhat concerned”; and 100 denoted “always concerned.”

The average response among respondents was 53, indicating that the surveyed foreigners are, collectively speaking, “somewhat concerned” about fluctuations in the USD:MXN exchange rate.

In general, fluctuations in the exchange rate are more of a concern now for foreigners in Mexico than in years gone by because, over a period spanning decades, the value of the peso against the US dollar trended down. However, in recent years the peso has bucked that trend, appreciating more than 10% against the greenback between 2021 and 2025, and continuing to strengthen this year.

A majority of respondents have loaned money in Mexico

Over half of the survey respondents have loaned money locally while living in Mexico.

Around 22% of respondents have loaned an amount under US $500, while 20% have lent between $500 and $3,000. About 11.5% of respondents have lent over $3,000 to someone in Mexico. Those three percentages add up to about 53.5%.

The remaining 46.5% of surveyed foreigners haven’t lent money to anyone while living in Mexico.

15% is the most common restaurant tip rate among respondents

Almost 48% of respondents typically tip “roughly 15%” of their total bill at restaurants in Mexico.

Almost 30% of surveyed foreigners usually tip “roughly 20%” when eating out, while 18.5% typically leave gratuities of “roughly 10%” of their total bill.

Just over 2% of respondents typically tip more than 20% of their total restaurant bill, while just under 2% usually tip less than 10%.

Your say

We asked survey respondents to provide additional information if they have experienced money issues with contractors and/or service providers in Mexico or if they have been a victim of a financial crime here. Many of the survey respondents who said they have been a victim of a financial crime recounted stories of being mugged, pickpocketed or having money stolen from their homes.

Below is a (lightly edited) selection of the comments we received.

Money issues with contractors

I paid for materials I didn’t get.

The price changed during the project due to the number of man-hours worked.

I had disagreements over what was included with certain construction costs. The disagreements arose from familiarity with what is typical in the U.S. versus what is typical in Mexico.

I paid for products and services I never received.

I didn’t receive reimbursement for a shoddy job.

I paid upfront for work that never happened or was executed poorly.

The contractor demanded more money than we agreed on.

The contractor failed to complete work and stole building materials.

Money issues with contractors and providers of regular services

A cleaning lady we had for eight years was stealing money from our purse and wallets during the whole time she was working for us.

A landlord kept my 20,000-peso security deposit without cause.

In order to continue having hot water in the apartment, I had to purchase equipment and pay for the installation because the landlord would not.

My rent increased above the agreed-upon rate. The increase was much higher than the standard rate increase in San Miguel de Allende.

The gardener wanted more money and simply stopped working until he got his raise.

I’m a former timeshare owner and the maintenance fee was immediately doubled after I was informed it was being adjusted because it was unfair. This was almost 20 years ago. It was extremely intimidating and I was threatened. Now that we know about cartel involvement in timeshares, I am so glad we got out even though we had to pay US $10,000.

My landlord insisted on me paying rent in US dollars, then stopped when the dollar weakened. The landlord greatly increased my rent, specifically saying, “My expenses have gone up because of inflation and the dollar isn’t worth as much.” She then converted the rent from dollars into pesos, increasing it by 20%.

I have had minor issues but have always been able to work them out. That’s life anywhere.

Financial crimes in Mexico

I was a victim of fraud when purchasing a car.

I was mugged. I lost my phone and wallet.

I was robbed of money, jewelry and a tablet by a “nurse” taking care of me.

Someone hacked my virtual HSBC card and ran up unauthorized charges.

I was the victim of the fraudulent sale of a timeshare.

An employee of a Mexican bank was siphoning funds and using new deposits to cover withdrawals. She was caught. I had to testify against her in exchange for the bank honoring my account balance.

I was coerced into a timeshare purchase.

A vacation rental that I paid for in advance was not owned or managed by the guy who rented it to me.

I was a victim of a credit card scam in a taxi.

A fruit vendor gave me counterfeit money.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Court Targets Illegal Land Use at Playa Dominical
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Constitutional Court has ordered the Municipality of Osa to do more to remove unapproved businesses and makeshift structures from public beachfront land at Playa Dominical. The court issued the order after receiving a complaint that the local government had not fully followed an earlier ruling from November 2025. The latest decision was issued a couple of days ago on the 18th.

The order applies to Osa Mayor Mainor Anchía Angulo and Daniela López Rivera, the acting head of the municipal department responsible for managing public coastal land. They must take the necessary steps to deal with the structures and businesses that remain in the protected beach area.

The judges warned that the case could be sent to prosecutors if municipal officials continue to fall short of the court’s order. The dispute involves makeshift homes, tents, canopies, sales stands and other structures set up on public land near the beach without permission. Residents and legally registered businesses say these activities block public space and create disorder along one of Dominical’s busiest beachfront areas.

The court first ruled on the case on November 14, 2025. It gave the municipality four months to inspect the area and take the steps needed to protect the public beach zone. That deadline passed on March 14, 2026 and Municipal officials say they have not ignored the problem. An inspection on February 20 found about 30 commercial stands along a 300-meter section of the beachfront.

On March 6, people operating businesses without permission reportedly left the area voluntarily. Municipal workers then removed makeshift structures and ropes, cleaned the beach and installed 19 signs explaining the rules for using public coastal land. The municipality carried out another operation on May 13 with help from the Tourist Police. Officials found tents, temporary structures and other unapproved uses of the beach area. Some of the people found there had already received warnings during an earlier operation.

Another operation took place on August 13. However, some people reportedly returned the following day. The Constitutional Court found that these operations had not solved the problem. Municipal officials also acknowledged that they had not found a lasting solution. The Municipality of Osa told the court that it is preparing a larger operation involving the Public Force, Immigration Police, the National System of Conservation Areas, environmental prosecutors and the Health Ministry.

The plan could include more inspections, removal operations and possible legal cases against people found using public beachfront land without permission. Costa Rican law limits private construction and business activity on protected beachfront land. Local governments are responsible for inspecting these areas, keeping them open to the public and acting when someone uses them without approval.

Playa Dominical is one of Costa Rica’s best-known surfing destinations and this case highlights the difficult balance between informal businesses, public beach access and the responsibility of local governments to manage popular coastal areas. The Municipality of Osa has not announced when its next operation will take place.

World.title: Costa Rica Lawmakers Challenge Sweeping State-Secrecy Order
World.content:
Opposition lawmakers asked Costa Rica’s Constitutional Chamber today to immediately suspend a decree that places broad categories of government security information, including budgets and public contracts, under state secrecy. Lawmakers from the National Liberation Party, Broad Front, Social Christian Unity Party and the Citizen Agenda Coalition filed a constitutional challenge against the Executive Decree.

The filing argues that the decree violates constitutional protections covering the public’s right to request and access government information. It asks the court to suspend the measure while judges determine whether it is constitutional. The lawmakers accept that operational plans, intelligence and other sensitive security information may require protection. Their objection centers on the decree’s wider reach, particularly its coverage of spending, procurement procedures, bids, contracts and administrative decisions.

According to the opposition, those restrictions could prevent journalists, legislators and the public from monitoring how government money is spent. The filing argues that secrecy should remain an exceptional and narrowly justified measure rather than becoming a general rule for government security operations.

The opposition’s challenge joins four earlier cases filed by citizens. As of Monday, the Constitutional Chamber was reviewing the admissibility of three appeals for constitutional protection and one separate constitutional challenge. The latest filing does not automatically suspend the decree. Costa Rican constitutional law generally allows a disputed regulation to remain in effect while judges examine a challenge unless the court orders otherwise.

President Laura Fernández signed the decree on July 27, and it was published in the official La Gaceta newspaper on August 10. The measure covers information connected to the National Public Security Council, the Directorate of Intelligence and National Security, known as DIS, and the government security group called Fuerza Élite.

It also applies to other security and national defense coordination led by the presidency. Protected material includes reports, recordings, meeting minutes, operational plans, command structures, intelligence methods, technological resources and police response strategies. The decree also covers procurement records, including technical studies, offers, contract awards, financing arrangements and the execution of contracts.

Government employees, advisers and private contractors who work with the covered agencies must maintain confidentiality. That obligation continues indefinitely, including after their employment or contractual relationship with the government ends. Fernández has defended the measure, saying publicly available information related to national security will remain accessible. She said the decree is intended to protect information that would be dangerous for criminal organizations to obtain.

The president cited organized-crime strategies and the identities of people or companies hired to conduct polygraph testing as examples of information that could expose officials or contractors to threats. The government has argued that disclosing sensitive information could compromise police operations, endanger officials and interfere with international security cooperation.

Opposition lawmakers say the decree goes much further than protecting active investigations or police tactics. The Constitutional Chamber must now decide whether to accept the latest challenge and whether to grant the requested suspension.

World.title: Costa Rica flood emergency keeps 473 schools closed and 1,300 people in shelters
World.content:
If you were thinking of or had plan to go to Caribbean side or in the Northern Zone this week, the heavy rain may have stopped but the disruption has not. Classes remain suspended at 473 schools, and more than 1,300 people are still living in 23 temporary shelters four days after Tropical Wave #33 pushed already-swollen rivers past their banks. Emergency crews are still reaching communities they could not get to over the weekend.

The Education Ministry closure list covers seven education regions. Sarapiquí accounts for 138 schools closed outright, Guápiles for 131 on partial suspension and Sulá for 110, with smaller numbers in Turrialba, Zona Norte-Norte, Limón and Cartago. That is a sharp drop from Monday, when 990 schools were shut. The ministry says the list changes daily and asks families to check its official channels rather than secondhand reports, because a school can reopen and close again within hours.

The rain itself has eased. The National Meteorological Institute expects only isolated showers on the Caribbean coast and variable downpours in the Northern Zone through the morning, with scattered afternoon rain reaching the Central Valley, the Central Pacific and the South Pacific, and possible showers on the Nicoya Peninsula.

The risk that remains is in the ground, not the sky. Soil across the Caribbean and the South Pacific is saturated, which means an ordinary afternoon shower can now trigger a landslide or push a river back up with almost no warning. A hillside that held all season can fail on a rainfall total that would normally pass without incident.

The weekend produced some of the heaviest rain on record. Nine weather stations set 24-hour precipitation records between 7 a.m. Sunday and 7 a.m. Monday, according to preliminary Institute data, with eight of them on the Caribbean slope.

Roxana de Pococí recorded 263.4 millimeters (10.4 inches) in a single day. For comparison, a heavy Costa Rican downpour typically drops around 60 millimeters (2.4 inches) over three hours. The Fundación Neotrópica station in Sierpe de Osa, on the Pacific side, logged 134.6 millimeters (5.3 inches).

Across 48 hours, the Caribbean and parts of the Northern Zone took between 200 and 360 millimeters (7.9 and 14.2 inches). At some stations a single weekend delivered half of what August normally brings in a full month, and monthly totals elsewhere have already reached between 100 and 170 percent of the historical average with almost two weeks still to go.

The National Emergency Commission is still supplying communities it cannot reach by road. A helicopter has been running food deliveries to the indigenous territories of Tayní Cabécar and Alto Chirripó in Limón, and to communities in Sarapiquí, where damaged roads and bridges have cut off vehicle access.

People in shelters are receiving meals, bedding, hygiene kits and medical checks. The count has stayed above 1,300 since Monday and will keep shifting as some families go home and others are evacuated. Route 32, the main link between San José and Limón, was closed Tuesday afternoon after material fell onto the roadway, and the Public Works Ministry scheduled an inspection for first thing Wednesday. Whether it reopens depends on what crews found.

If you need to reach the Caribbean, Route 10 through Turrialba is the alternate and is open to all vehicle types, though it has taken closures of its own during this rain cycle. Check the ministry’s channels before you leave rather than after you are on the road, because the Zurquí stretch can shut again within minutes of a downpour.

Do not drive through standing water, however shallow it looks. Moving water just 30 centimeters (12 inches) deep can float a car, and on a flooded road you cannot see whether the surface underneath is still there. If you have anything booked or scheduled in Sarapiquí, Tortuguero, Cahuita, Puerto Viejo or Guápiles, call ahead. Access varies community by community, and people on the ground will know whether the road to their door is open well before any official list catches up.

The forecast calls for lighter rain in the days ahead. But with the ground this saturated and most of the rainy season still to come, conditions on the Caribbean slope can change a good deal faster than the forecast suggests.

World.title: Man in wheelchair slashed with machete on Philip Goldson Highway
World.content:
Man in wheelchair slashed with machete on Philip Goldson Highway

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Police are looking for a San Jose Village man after a physically incapacitated resident was chopped on the Philip Goldson Highway Sunday night.

According to the report, a 43 year old unemployed man was heading home in his wheelchair around 9:45pm when he heard someone call his name in front of a church in the village.

He turned and saw a man he has known for more than 20 years, dressed in a black shirt and red short pants, holding two machetes.

The man approached and began lashing him all over his body with one of the machetes, leaving two cut wounds to the head, one to the back and another above the right ear, along with bruises to the left wrist.

The attacker ran off when neighbours came out to assist. An ambulance took the injured man to the Northern Regional Hospital for treatment.

His injuries were certified as wounding by a doctor.

The complainant told police that street lights in the area were bright and he positively recognised his attacker. William Suchete of San Jose Village is wanted for the offence.

World.title: Deputy Prime Minister Cordel Hyde celebrates 53rd birthday
World.content:
Deputy Prime Minister Cordel Hyde celebrates 53rd birthday

By Zoila Palma: Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Natural Resources Cordel Hyde is celebrating his 53rd birthday today, marking another year in a political career spanning more than two decades.

Hyde’s journey in public service began in journalism at Amandala newspaper, founded by his father, Evan X Hyde, before he entered national politics in 1998.

That year, he defeated then-UDP incumbent Hubert Elrington to become the Lake Independence Area Representative.

Since then, Hyde has remained a prominent figure in Belizean politics, maintaining a strong presence in Lake Independence, apart from a brief period away from elected office between 2012 and 2015.

He has also served in several key Cabinet positions, including Minister of Education and Housing under the Said Musa administration.

Hyde’s public and personal journey has included both political achievements and significant challenges, including the heartbreaking loss of his son, Khalid, to cancer.

Today, as Minister of Natural Resources, Hyde has focused on reforming the Lands Ministry and rebuilding public confidence in an institution that has faced longstanding concerns over its operations.

He is recognized for his perseverance and continued commitment to public service and national development.

World.title: Restaurant argument over broken beer ends with choking and $600 shades destroyed
World.content:
Restaurant argument over broken beer ends with choking and $600 shades destroyed

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 50 year old cowboy of Indian Church Village has been charged with harm and damage to property following an altercation at a village restaurant.

According to the report, a 45 year old boat captain went to the restaurant on Friday and ordered a beer at the bar. As the bartender handed it to him, the bottle fell and broke.

A man at the restaurant shouted that he had to pay for it. The complainant responded that he never touched the beer and would not pay.

He told police a man he has known for over twenty years then jumped up from a table, grabbed him by the throat with both hands and began choking him. Several patrons tried to intervene without success.

He was then pushed to the ground, hitting his head, before the man climbed on top of him and choked him a second time. Patrons managed to pull the man off.

A pair of shades valued at $600 hanging around the complainant’s neck was broken in half during the attack.

Santiago Escalante was arrested and charged on Tuesday. He chose to remain silent.

World.title: Orange Walk driver charged with DUI after two vehicle crash
World.content:
Orange Walk driver charged with DUI after two vehicle crash

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 58 year old technician of San Lorenzo Road has been charged with driving under the influence following a crash on Otro Benque Road on Sunday evening.

Police responded to the scene around 7:45pm and found a blue 2010 Ford Escape parked on the right shoulder of the road with minor damage to its front right bumper, fender and wheel.

About 50 feet away was a black Mazda B2500 pickup that had collided with a wooden BEL lamp post. The pickup sustained extensive damage to its front right side and passenger side, and its right front wheel was found some 25 feet from the vehicle. The post was left slightly tilted but undamaged.

Initial investigation revealed the pickup driver was travelling from Orange Walk Town toward San Lorenzo Housing Site when he struck the parked Ford Escape, lost control and crashed into the lamp post.

No one was injured.

Police detected the aroma of alcohol on the driver’s breath at the scene. He was detained and later provided a urine sample at the station.

Oswaldo Vasquez was charged with driving under the influence and driving without due care and attention. He was granted police bail of $600.

World.title: BELTRAIDE highlights MSMEs as key to Rural Economic growth
World.content:
BELTRAIDE highlights MSMEs as key to Rural Economic growth

By Zoila Palma: BELTRAIDE CEO Narda Garcia has highlighted the important role of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) in driving economic development across Belize, particularly in rural communities.

Garcia made the remarks during the Ministry of Rural Transformation, Community Development and Local Government’s Annual Stakeholder Recognition Awards 2026, which recognized partners contributing to socioeconomic development at the village, town and municipal levels.

BELTRAIDE noted that rural transformation and MSME development are closely connected, as entrepreneurs in communities create jobs, add value to local resources and strengthen local economies when they have access to training, financing, markets and other business support.

BELTRAIDE said fostering entrepreneurship, investor confidence and business growth remains central to its mission of supporting Belize’s socioeconomic development.

In addition, BELTRAIDE also highlighted the National MSME Roadshow, now in its third year, which brings business development services directly to entrepreneurs across the country.

BELTRAIDE commended Minister of Rural Transformation, Community Development and Local Government Oscar Requena and CEO Valentino Shal for their continued partnership in promoting community-centered development.

World.title: Man wanted after teen reports sexual threats at Orange Walk market
World.content:
Man wanted after teen reports sexual threats at Orange Walk market

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Police are investigating a report of sexual harassment made by a 17 year old student at the Orange Walk market on Sunday morning.

According to the report, the student was standing outside her mother’s market stall around 9:34am having a conversation with another woman when a man she has known by an alias for five years approached and made explicit sexual remarks toward her, along with a threat to sexually assault her wherever he saw her.

She told police the remarks made her uncomfortable and she warned him she would call the police. When she took out her phone and acted as though she was calling, he picked up a wooden chair from another market stall and moved to throw it at her.

The woman with her intervened and began recording him. He put the chair down but continued shouting at her to stop recording, saying he was not afraid of the burial ground or jail, before leaving the area.

The student made the report at the Orange Walk Police Station accompanied by her mother. Statements were recorded from both and a copy of the video footage was obtained.

Checks were made at the market but the man could not be located. The matter remains under investigation.

World.title: PSU President sounds alarm over Revenue Authority bill: “That is dangerous”
World.content:
PSU President sounds alarm over Revenue Authority bill: “That is dangerous”

By Zoila Palma: Public Service Union (PSU) President Dean Flowers is raising serious concerns about the proposed Revenue Authority Bill, warning that the legislation could place too much power in the hands of one government minister.

The bill, tabled in the House of Representatives at the end of July, forms part of the government’s plan to transform the Belize Tax Service into a Semi-Autonomous Revenue Authority (SARA).

While employees and members of the business community have already voiced concerns about the proposed changes, Flowers says his biggest worry is not workers’ pensions or how public officers will be transferred into the new authority, but rather the proposed system of checks and balances.

“For me as a citizen, the most dangerous defect in the draft revenue authority bill has nothing to do with pensions and workers protection,” Flowers told 7News Belize.

The PSU president said that the proposed advisory board would have limited authority and would not be able to direct the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) or make operational decisions.

He said the bill instead places significant authority in the hands of the minister responsible for the authority, who would appoint and remove the CEO. “All the power instead flows from one person, a minister who appoints and removes the CEO,” Flowers stated.

Flowers also questioned the process for selecting the future CEO, arguing that there should be an independent and competitive process to determine the person’s qualifications and integrity.

He said the advisory board should have a meaningful role in assessing the individual who will lead the Revenue Authority. “We must ensure that the manner in which the CEO of the soon to be Revenue Authority is established that there is a clear and competitive process,” he said.

The PSU president further warned that the proposed arrangement could have broader implications for how statutory bodies are governed in Belize.

Under the current proposal, Flowers said, the CEO would need the minister’s approval to take action, while the minister could issue instructions to the CEO. “If the CEO wants to do something, he seeks the approval of the minister. If the minister wants to do something, he instructs the CEO. And that is dangerous.”

World.title: BNTU President: “Teachers are becoming discouraged,” leaving classrooms
World.content:
BNTU President: “Teachers are becoming discouraged,” leaving classrooms

By Zoila Palma: Belize National Teachers’ Union (BNTU) President Nadia Caliz is raising concerns over what she says are growing challenges affecting teachers, including educators leaving classrooms, unclear employment status and delays in professional licensing.

Caliz says these issues are contributing to frustration and discouragement among teachers across the education system.

Caliz explained that more teachers are leaving classroom positions and applying for Participate Learning but their existing posts remain available. She said some new teachers are then brought in under temporary employment arrangements without being properly informed of their status. “When you come in, you come in on what you call temporary employment,” Caliz said, adding that some teachers only discover they are not in full-time positions when they seek leave, benefits or appointment.

The BNTU president also criticized delays in the processing and renewal of teachers’ licenses. According to Caliz, some educators have been forced to leave their classrooms because their licenses were not issued on time, despite the delays being outside the teachers’ control. “What kind of nonsense is that?” she said.

Caliz also called on school managers to engage more closely with the union. She said the BNTU has made multiple attempts to meet with major school managements, including government, Catholic and Methodist schools, but some general managers did not attend. “It’s important that we meet, it’s important that we discuss,” she said.

The BNTU president further pushed back against accusations that the union is biased, saying the organization seeks to hear management’s side before raising concerns. “We come to you to get your side,” Caliz said.

World.title: Assault on tax dodgers!
World.content:
Owners of 432 delinquent properties in the Half-Way-Tree area are about to come under closer scrutiny as the Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation (KSAMC) and Tax Administration Jamaica (TAJ) take their tax compliance campaign into the busy commercial district today in pursuit of $162 million in unpaid property taxes.

The three-day field operation forms part of the third phase of an 11-month joint revenue drive aimed at improving compliance and recovering outstanding property taxes, trade licence fees, and signs-and-billboards obligations.

The campaign follows an intelligence-gathering exercise in which the two agencies compiled information on property owners, businesses, trade licences, and other commercial obligations in the Half-Way-Tree area.

Kingston Mayor Andrew Swaby said the information gathered has revealed the extent of the problem, with some property tax arrears stretching back many years.

“Excluding the current financial year 2026-2027, there are 432 properties in the Half-Way-Tree area with property tax arrears going back six years totalling $162 million. Of those 432 properties, 151 are associated with businesses accounting for $96 million of that total. On the trade licence side, 195 businesses are registered in this category in the selected area with estimated arrears of $48 million,” he said, during a press conference on Tuesday.

According to the mayor, the operation is intended to improve compliance while ensuring that businesses meet their statutory obligation to pay taxes and fees.

“Let me be clear about the tone and intent of this initiative: This is not an exercise in harassment. It’s an exercise in fairness and accountability. Every one of us has a statutory obligation to pay our taxes, and we intend to see that obligation met. When legitimate business owners pay their fair share, it is unfair for the others operating alongside them to benefit from the same public infrastructure, road rehabilitation, street lighting, public sanitation, drain cleaning, and municipal park maintenance, without contributing to its upkeep,” he noted.

Over the next three days, field teams will be visiting businesses and providing information and guidance to operators on how to bring their accounts up to date.

The area has been divided into three zones to facilitate the exercise.

Zone One covers Hagley Park, Eastwood Park Road, Red Hills Road, Westminster Road, Lower Sandringham Avenue, and Woodglen Drive.

Zone Two includes Hope Road North, Surbiton Road, Waterloo Avenue, West King’s House Road, Constant Spring Road, North Avenue, Central Avenue, South Avenue, Merrick Avenue, Ellesmere Road, Suthermere Road, and North Odeon Avenue.

Zone Three covers Half-Way-Tree Road, Balmoral Avenue, Maxfield Avenue, Hagley Park, Hope Road South, Winchester Road, Ruthven Road, Skibo Avenue, Bradley Avenue, Ballater Avenue, Cargill Avenue, Cecelio Avenue, Stratham Avenue and Clock Tower Plaza Road.

Rather than simply asking delinquent operators to report to municipal offices, the agencies are taking services directly into the commercial area.

A temporary customer service desk will operate at Constant Spring Arcade from 10:30 am to 2:00 pm each day during the three-day exercise. Property owners and business operators will be able to get help registering for online payments, obtain printed copies of official trade licences, settle payments, regularise signs and billboards approvals, and resolve account queries.

The approach is intended to make it easier for businesses to address outstanding obligations while giving them an opportunity to get clarification and assistance without travelling to central municipal offices.

TAJ Deputy Commissioner General for Operations Dave Jeffrey said the Half-Way-Tree operation builds on similar joint exercises the agency has carried out with municipalities in St James, Portmore and St Catherine.

He said those operations had produced significant improvements in compliance, with some areas moving from rates as low as 25 per cent to as high as 75 per cent by the end of the intervention.

Jeffrey said the agencies are aiming for an even stronger result in Half-Way-Tree.

“For this operation, we have expanded our focus beyond property tax to include trade and business licences and the signs and billboards. The operation covers an 11-month period and is slated to end in March 2027, and by that time, we’re aiming that the collection rate will go up to at least 85 per cent of the outstanding property taxes and trade and business licences arrears,” he said.

The three-day outreach is not the end of the campaign. It is part of a four-phase process that will move from planning and intelligence-gathering to direct interaction with taxpayers and, ultimately, enforcement.

According to Jeffrey, the agencies are deliberately trying to change the way businesses approach tax payments by encouraging them to use online services.

“For the interactive session, we are encouraging business operators to make their payments online. As a result, we will not be having a mobile bus for the interactive session. These are business and commercial entities, and we really want them to utilise the online payment and hence why we won’t be having the mobile unit… We want to change that culture and that habit of tax payment and we’ll be doing everything to facilitate that process,” he said.

During the interactive phase, TAJ will serve notices, provide support to taxpayers, facilitate online queries, and engage directly with businesses to help them address outstanding obligations. Compliant taxpayers will also be recognised with congratulatory certificates as part of the initiative.

World.title: No more moos
World.content:
Moo Moo was injured in a hit and run along Walks Road in Spanish Town, St Catherine. Naphtali Junior

AFTER days lying in the sun as residents did their best to provide the care she needed, Moo Moo’s story has come to a heartbreaking end.

The injured cow, who captured the hearts of residents on Walks Road in Spanish Town, was euthanised by the Veterinary Services Division on Wednesday after the professionals determined her injuries were too severe.

Reports are that the cow was injured in a hit-and-run incident on August 11. Residents said they made several reports and calls to animal-related facilities, but were unable to get assistance for the animal. Gabriel Hamilton and Nicholas Thomas became the beloved animal’s primary caregivers, staying with her until her final moments.

The animal’s owner has not come forward.
